dimension: Enterprise / organization surface (organizations, organization_* schema, /enterprise portal, /api/admin/organization[s]/*)
summary: The enterprise surface is the platform's largest piece of under-exercised machinery: ~9,200 lines across 35 API routes, 11 portal pages, 6 services, 13 tables, 76 indexes and 27 RLS policies — serving exactly ONE organization holding 17 rows in total, with fewer than 50 recorded query executions across the whole 120-day pg_stat_statements window (2026-05-07 → now). Its money core (wallet, ledger, dual journal, disbursement maker-checker) is genuinely built and correct-looking; what is broken or dead is everything around it. The organization SMS billing subsystem has never processed a single message and its daily grant job is a structural no-op that can never fire; one job handler queries a column that does not exist; one API route and its 71-line service method have zero callers; a customer-facing "API & Webhooks" page mints fake `ky_live_*` credentials entirely in browser state; and the portal splits the same six endpoints across two incompatible React Query key namespaces so that the Funding Portal's write mutations invalidate nothing the other pages read. Per-request efficiency is also structurally lossy: every `withDb` costs 6 fixed round-trips and the org services call it two or three times per request, including on cache hits.

findings.title: /enterprise/api-keys is a live nav item backed 100% by client-side mock data — it mints fake ky_live_* credentials in browser state
findings.evidence: app/(enterprise)/enterprise/api-keys/page.tsx:17 `import { apiKeys as seedKeys, webhooks as seedHooks } from '../../_data'`; :41-48 `generate()` builds `ky_live_${randomToken(28)}` from Math.random (:19-20) and pushes it into React state only — no fetch, no mutation. app/(enterprise)/_data.ts:6-9 states plainly "API keys and webhooks stay mock: there is no developer-settings backend yet (no API key issuance, no webhook delivery pipeline)". Confirmed in DB: no api_keys/webhooks table exists among the 13 organization_* tables. The disabled-nav mechanism EXISTS (components/shared/portal-sidebar.tsx:30 `soon?: boolean`, :266-270 renders it disabled with a "Coming soon" pill) but app/(enterprise)/layout.tsx:30-66 sets `soon` on ZERO items — so :61 `{ href: '/enterprise/api-keys', label: 'API & Webhooks' }` presents as a shipped feature. Mock webhook URLs point at a third party ('https://api.hisa.africa/hooks/kitabu', _data.ts:38).
findings.impact: A B2B customer-facing portal hands an enterprise coordinator a string that looks exactly like a production API credential, records it in a table with 'active' status and a fake 'last used 2 min ago', and lets them 'revoke' it — none of which touches a server. Any integration built against it fails silently; any support ticket about it is unanswerable. 214 lines of page + 41 lines of seed data is dead weight on top.
findings.recommendation: Set `soon: true` on the API & Webhooks nav item (layout.tsx:61) so PortalSidebar renders it disabled, and gate the page body behind the same flag — this is a one-line change using machinery that already exists. Delete app/(enterprise)/_data.ts and the page when the decision is that no developer surface is coming.

findings.title: The enterprise portal uses two incompatible React Query key namespaces for the same six endpoints, so Funding Portal writes invalidate nothing the other pages read
findings.evidence: Same endpoint, two keys: /organization/dashboard → ['enterprise','dashboard'] (app/(enterprise)/enterprise/page.tsx:47) vs ['organization','dashboard'] (funding/page.tsx:135). /organization/groups → ['enterprise','groups'] (page.tsx:51, branches/page.tsx:24, disbursements/page.tsx:79) vs ['organization','groups'] (funding/page.tsx:142). /organization/accounting → ['enterprise','accounting'] (reports/page.tsx:202) vs ['organization','accounting'] (funding/page.tsx:155). programs?report=budget → ['enterprise','reports','budget'] (reports/page.tsx:47) vs ['organization','budget-report'] (funding/page.tsx:161). programs?report=donor → ['enterprise','reports','donor'] (reports/page.tsx:129) vs ['organization','donor-report'] (funding/page.tsx:167). /organization/disbursements → ['enterprise','disbursements',page] (disbursements/page.tsx:87) vs ['organization','disbursements'] (funding/page.tsx:149). Every write mutation in funding/page.tsx invalidates the prefix ['organization'] only — :191 (setPolicy), :574 (deposit), :649 (createProgram), :801 (disburse) — which matches none of the ['enterprise', …] keys. reports/page.tsx:60-62 and :340-342 invalidate ['enterprise','reports',…], which matches none of funding's keys.
findings.impact: After a coordinator deposits capital, creates a funding program, or disburses money in the Funding Portal, the Portfolio page KPIs, the Disbursements page wallet tile (['enterprise','wallet'], disbursements/page.tsx:75) and the Reports page budget/donor tables all keep showing pre-write figures until their own staleTime lapses or the user hard-reloads — i.e. the portal displays stale money numbers immediately after a money movement. Separately, navigating Portfolio ⇄ Funding Portal refetches dashboard, groups, accounting, budget and donor reports even though an identical fresh copy is already cached, doubling requests, serverless invocations and DB connections for those six endpoints.
findings.recommendation: Collapse to one namespace (a shared `organizationKeys` factory in hooks/, mirroring hooks/use-members.ts's memberKeys pattern already used elsewhere in this codebase) and point every enterprise page and every invalidateQueries call at it. Also set a consistent staleTime — disbursements/page.tsx:74-88 sets none, so it defaults to 0 and refetches on every mount and window focus, while funding/page.tsx uses 30s.

findings.title: lib/jobs/handlers.ts:1014 queries organization_members.is_active — a column that does not exist — so any organization-payer low-balance alert throws and retries forever
findings.evidence: lib/jobs/handlers.ts:1012-1017: `SELECT m.email FROM organization_members om JOIN members m ON m.id = om.member_id WHERE om.organization_id = $1 AND om.is_active AND om.org_role = 'lead' …`. Live prod information_schema for public.organization_members returns columns: id, organization_id, member_id, org_role, status (text), invited_by, joined_at, archived_at, archived_by, created_at, updated_at — there is NO is_active column. Control run to prove the correct predicate resolves: `SELECT count(*) FROM organization_members om WHERE om.status='active'` → 2. The query is not wrapped in try/catch (only the queueEmail call at :1021-1026 has a .catch); the withAdminDb call at :1010 propagates. Every other reader of this table uses status: lib/services/organization-plan.service.ts:191, :266.
findings.impact: The organization branch of handleSmsLowBalanceAlert raises SQLSTATE 42703 the first time it runs, failing the job, which then retries — feeding the job_queue backlog that is already this platform's single largest cost centre. Latent today only because no org-payer SMS has ever been sent (sms_usage_logs has 0 rows with payer_type='organization'); job_queue shows sms_low_balance_alert has run 3 times, all on 2026-08-07, all on the group branch.
findings.recommendation: Change `om.is_active` to `om.status = 'active'` at lib/jobs/handlers.ts:1014. One-word fix; add a unit test asserting the org branch executes against a real schema, since tsc cannot catch a column name inside a SQL string literal.

findings.title: The organization SMS billing subsystem has never processed a message, and its daily grant job is a no-op that cannot fire for two independent reasons
findings.evidence: sms_usage_logs grouped by payer_type over all 401 rows: group 390, platform 11, organization 0 — zero org-attributed sends have EVER occurred (first log 2026-05-29, last 2026-09-03). organization_billing_accounts: 0 live rows (2 dead). organization_sms_credits: 0 live rows (7 dead). job_queue shows type `organization_sms_allowance_grant` with 70 rows, all status 'completed', one per day from 2026-08-21 01:00 to 2026-09-03 22:00. Its query (lib/services/organization-plan.service.ts:336-349) INNER JOINs organization_billing_accounts — with zero rows in that table the join can never produce a row; pg_stat_statements confirms 70 calls, rows=0, every time. Independently, the only organization's subscription has sms_allowance_included = 0.00 (organization_subscriptions row for EZZAHCOMM, plan premium_plus), which the `s.sms_allowance_included > $2` predicate also excludes. Dead surface hanging off this: 5 tables, addOrganizationSmsCredits/getOrganizationSmsBilling/setOrganizationSmsRate (lib/services/billing.service.ts:772-930), two top-up routes (app/api/admin/organization/sms-credits/route.ts, app/api/admin/organizations/[id]/sms-credits/route.ts), the Billing page top-up UI (app/(enterprise)/enterprise/billing/page.tsx:38-160), and the admin revenue rollup getOrganizationUsage (lib/services/sms-margin.service.ts:217-244), two of whose four correlated subqueries read the permanently-empty organization_sms_credits.
findings.impact: A daily scheduled job that provably cannot ever grant anything, plus ~400 lines of billing code, 5 tables, 12 indexes and a customer-facing top-up form that have never moved a single credit. The cost in ms is negligible (112ms total over 70 runs); the cost is that this is a check that cannot fail — nobody will ever learn from it whether org allowances work, and the first real org SMS customer will exercise all of it cold.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) prove the path end-to-end once — assign a plan with sms_allowance_included > 0 so grantSmsAllowanceInTx bootstraps the billing account, then send one org-payer message and verify the debit — or (b) stop scheduling organization_sms_allowance_grant until an organization actually holds an allowance. Change the INNER JOIN at organization-plan.service.ts:338 to a LEFT JOIN so an org with an allowance but no billing-account row is not silently skipped.

findings.title: GET /api/admin/organization/reports and organizationService.getGroupDetail (71 lines, 3 queries) have zero callers
findings.evidence: app/api/admin/organization/reports/route.ts is the only handler for that path; the sole client reference is lib/api/endpoints.ts:583 `detail: (groupId) => adminApi.get('/organization/reports?groupId=' + groupId)`. A repo-wide grep for `organizationApi.detail` and for `.detail\b` across app/, components/, hooks/, lib/ and __tests__/ returns no call site (the `.detail` hits that exist are unrelated: memberKeys.detail, loanKeys.detail, marketing row.detail). The route's only service method, organizationService.getGroupDetail (lib/services/organization.service.ts:335-405), is 71 lines running three queries including a 4-LATERAL rollup and a 12-month contributions trend, and is reachable from nowhere else. pg_stat_statements over 120 days confirms no org-scoped execution.
findings.impact: 71 lines of service + a route + an endpoint entry that must be kept compiling, reviewed, and permission-audited (it carries its own 'organization.reports.view' permission string) for a feature no UI ever calls. It also duplicates listGroupSummaries' entire LATERAL block — two copies of the same fan-out-avoidance SQL that must be kept in sync.
findings.recommendation: Delete the route, getGroupDetail, and endpoints.ts:583 — or wire it to the Branches page's per-branch drill-down, which is presumably what it was built for. Do not leave it: the codebase's own comment at lib/auth/middleware.ts:128-134 documents exactly this hazard (a deleted-rather-than-orphaned guard, because 'it typechecks fine and reads plausibly, so the next route to be added would have reached for it').

findings.title: /organization/accounting opens two pooled connections and ships an `accounts` array that no consumer reads
findings.evidence: app/api/admin/organization/accounting/route.ts:16-20 runs `Promise.all([listAccounts(ctx), getTrialBalance(ctx)])`. Both are separate `withDb` calls (lib/services/organization-accounting.service.ts:70 and :81), each of which is a full BEGIN + 4× set_config + COMMIT plus the query (lib/db/index.ts:137-154, :121-131) — two pool checkouts, two transactions, ~15 round-trips — and both SELECT from the same organization_accounts rows with the same organization_id predicate. Every consumer types and uses only trialBalance: lib/api/endpoints.ts:621 `adminApi.get<{ trialBalance: OrgTrialBalanceLine[] }>`, app/(enterprise)/enterprise/funding/page.tsx:154 `useQuery<{ trialBalance: TrialBalanceLine[] }>`, app/(enterprise)/enterprise/reports/page.tsx:201-205 (`const lines = data?.trialBalance ?? []`). The accounts array is serialized and sent, then discarded.
findings.impact: Doubles the DB connections, transactions and set_config round-trips for this endpoint, and puts an unused payload on the wire — on a page (Funding Portal) that already fires seven parallel requests. Every trial-balance field is a pure projection of the accounts rows already fetched, so the second query is redundant even if the payload were wanted.
findings.recommendation: Drop listAccounts from the route and return only trialBalance from one withDb/one query. Keep listAccounts as a service method only if a caller appears; today it has exactly one caller, this route.

findings.title: Org services pay the 6-round-trip withDb tax two or three times per request, including on Redis cache hits
findings.evidence: lib/db/index.ts:137-154 opens a pool client, issues BEGIN, then setTenantLocals (:121-131) fires FOUR separate `SELECT set_config($1,$2,TRUE)` statements, then COMMIT — six round-trips of fixed overhead before any real query. Three org paths pay it multiple times: (1) organization-finance.service.ts:1204-1206 — getDashboard calls `this.getWallet(ctx)` (its own withDb at :507) and then a second withDb at :1206, so a dashboard costs ~15 round-trips where 9 would do. (2) :629-630 programBudgetReport and :693-694 donorSpendReport each run `await withDb(ctx, db => assertReportsAccess(db, orgId(ctx)))` OUTSIDE the `cached(...)` wrapper, then a second withDb inside it — so even a 100% Redis hit still pays a full connection + transaction + 4 set_config + the getEffectiveLimits query (organization-plan.service.ts:211-218). The Funding Portal loads both reports on every visit. (3) :1098-1118 approveDisbursement runs THREE sequential transactions across TWO pools: withTransaction on the tenant pool, then settleOrgDisbursement (:372) on the withAdminDb BYPASSRLS pool, then a third `withDb(ctx, db => fetchOrgDisbursement(db, id))` at :1118 purely to re-read the row that settle just UPDATEd at :492-497.
findings.impact: On the Supavisor SESSION-mode pooler each of these is a real connection checkout, and DB_POOL_MAX is shared. A single Funding Portal load currently costs roughly 8 pool checkouts and ~30 statements; ~40% of those statements are set_config/BEGIN/COMMIT overhead rather than work. The approve path also holds two connections on two different pools serially, and the tenant transaction commits before settlement runs — so a settle failure leaves an 'approved' row that was never settled.
findings.recommendation: (a) In getDashboard, inline the wallet SELECT into the existing withDb's Promise.all instead of calling getWallet. (b) Move assertReportsAccess INSIDE the cached closure, or cache the entitlement itself for the same TTL — a plan change taking 60s to take effect is a smaller cost than a mandatory connection on every cache hit. (c) Have settleOrgDisbursement's final UPDATE use `RETURNING *` and drop the third withDb at :1118 entirely.

findings.title: The Portfolio and Funding Portal pages compute the same per-group aggregates twice per load, in two separate connections
findings.evidence: getDashboard's group_stats CTE (lib/services/organization-finance.service.ts:1221-1247) computes, per linked group, active_members from group_members, total_savings from contributions, loan_portfolio and loans_disbursed from loans, and loans_repaid from loan_repayments — then SUMs them. listGroupSummaries (lib/services/organization.service.ts:141-199) computes the identical per-group values via four LATERALs over the same four tables. app/(enterprise)/enterprise/page.tsx:46-53 fetches BOTH (dashboard for the six KPI tiles at :91-96, groups for the top-5 table at :56-59); funding/page.tsx:134-146 fetches both too. The groups payload comes back with limit defaulting to 200 (organization.service.ts:127) and the Portfolio page uses exactly five rows of it.
findings.impact: Four child tables (group_members, contributions, loans, loan_repayments) are scanned twice per page load through two separate pooled connections, to produce numbers where one set is the arithmetic SUM of the other. The dashboard's entire `portfolio` block is derivable client-side from the groups array the page already holds. Cost is small today (37 group_members, 23 contributions, 4 loans) but it scales with tenant data, not with organization count.
findings.recommendation: Either drop the dashboard's portfolio rollup and sum the groups payload in the page (the KPI tiles at page.tsx:91-96 map 1:1 onto columns listGroupSummaries already returns), or have the dashboard return the per-group rows and let the page derive both views from one fetch.

findings.title: getOrganizationDetail scans every unassigned active group on the platform (LIMIT 500) on every super-admin org detail page load
findings.evidence: lib/services/admin-organizations.service.ts:176-186 — the third of four parallel queries: `SELECT g.id, g.name, g.group_code, g.type FROM public.groups g WHERE g.status='active' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM organization_group_access oga WHERE oga.group_id=g.id AND oga.organization_id=$1 AND oga.is_active) ORDER BY g.name LIMIT 500`. It is returned as `assignableGroups` (:200) on every call to the detail endpoint. app/(admin)/admin/organizations/[id]/page.tsx:77 fetches it unconditionally on mount, alongside three more independent queries — useOrgStaff (:82), useOrgInvitations (:88), useOrganizationPlan (:92) — for four HTTP round trips and four pooled connections per page view.
findings.impact: The query's cost scales with the platform's total group count, not with the organization being viewed, and it runs whether or not the operator intends to assign anything. It exists only to populate an assignment dropdown. Additionally useOrganizationPlan (organization-plan.service.ts:188-194) re-COUNTs organization_group_access for the same org that getOrganizationDetail's `ga` LATERAL (:66-73) already counted as group_count in the same page load.
findings.recommendation: Move assignableGroups behind the 'Assign group' action as a separate, search-parameterised endpoint (the admin group search at /api/admin/search already exists), and fold the plan-usage counts into getOrganizationDetail's existing LATERAL so the page needs one round trip fewer.

findings.title: 11 of 12 organization RLS policies re-evaluate STABLE helper functions per row — only organization_disbursements got the InitPlan wrapping
findings.evidence: pg_policies on live prod: the four organization_disbursements policies wrap every helper, e.g. organization_disbursements_select USING `((SELECT is_super_admin()) OR ((SELECT app_current_role())='organization_coordinator' AND organization_id=(SELECT app_current_organization_id())) OR group_id=(SELECT app_current_group_id()))`. Every other organization_* policy calls them bare — organizations_select, organization_group_access_select, organization_members_select, organization_ledger_all, organization_wallets_all, organization_accounts_all, organization_journal_entries_all, organization_journal_lines_all, organization_billing_accounts_all, organization_sms_credits_all, organization_subscriptions_select, organization_invitations_select. pg_proc confirms all five helpers (is_super_admin, app_current_role, app_current_organization_id, app_current_group_id, app_current_user_id) are STABLE with procost=100, so the unwrapped form is re-evaluated per candidate row rather than hoisted to an InitPlan. Supabase's own `auth_rls_initplan` lint does not flag these (it matches auth.uid()/current_setting patterns, not custom helpers) — the performance advisor reported 5 initplan hits, none on organization tables, so this is invisible to the tooling.
findings.impact: Every row scanned on these tables costs up to three extra function invocations at procost 100 each. Negligible at 17 rows, but organization_group_access is on a genuinely hot path — idx_scan 118 on idx_org_group_access_active, and the Configuration Service policy resolver runs `organization_id IN (SELECT organization_id FROM organization_group_access WHERE group_id=$4 AND is_active)` 101 times in the pgss window (63 + 38 calls). The fix pattern is already proven and applied on one table, which is exactly the state in which the next table added inherits the slow form.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the 12 policies to wrap every helper call in `(SELECT fn())`, copying the organization_disbursements form verbatim. Follow the codebase's own rule from CREATE OR REPLACE experience: re-verify grants and re-run get_advisors after the DDL.

findings.title: organization_subscriptions carries two overlapping permissive SELECT policies, both evaluated on every read
findings.evidence: pg_policies: `organization_subscriptions_admin_write` is declared FOR ALL with qual `is_super_admin()`, so it also applies to SELECT on top of `organization_subscriptions_select` (qual `is_super_admin() OR (app_current_role()='organization_coordinator' AND organization_id=app_current_organization_id())`). Supabase's performance advisor reports this as multiple_permissive_policies for all 7 roles (anon, app_tenant, authenticated, authenticator, cli_login_postgres, dashboard_user, supabase_privileged_role). The table is read on the entitlement path — idx_scan on idx_org_subscriptions_one_active = 71, the highest scan count of any organization_subscriptions index.
findings.impact: Postgres OR-combines and evaluates both policies for every row on every SELECT, doubling the is_super_admin() invocation on the one table that getEffectiveLimits, getOrganizationPlan, assertReportsAccess and assertWhiteLabelAccess all read. Small today; it is a permanent 2x on the entitlement hot path.
findings.recommendation: Narrow organization_subscriptions_admin_write to `FOR INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE` (or three separate policies) so only organization_subscriptions_select governs reads. Same treatment the disbursements table already received when its `_all` policy was split into _select/_insert/_update/_delete (visible in pg_stat_statements as DROP POLICY organization_disbursements_all).

findings.title: The organization staff-invitation subsystem has never created a single row in production
findings.evidence: organization_invitations on live prod: n_live_tup 0, n_dead_tup 0 — no row was ever inserted, not even one later deleted. pg_stat_statements over 120 days shows only the list query (`SELECT id, email, first_name, … FROM public.organization_invitations WHERE organization_id …`) with 3 calls, plus DDL. The 2 live organization_members rows were therefore created via the direct addOrgStaff path (lib/services/organization-members.service.ts:133), not the invite flow. Unexercised surface: 5 public routes (app/api/v1/organization-invitations/{lookup,confirm-email,verify-otp,complete,decline}, 110 lines total), 4 admin routes (staff/invite, staff/invitations, .../[invitationId], .../resend), ~275 lines of service (organization-members.service.ts:265-540: createOrgInvitation, getOrgInvitation, confirmOrgInvitationEmail, verifyOrgInvitationOtp, listOrgInvitations, resendOrgInvitation, cancelOrgInvitation, declineOrgInvitationByToken, completeOrgInvitation), a 275-line accept page (app/(auth)/accept-org-invite/[token]/page.tsx), 4 indexes (3 with idx_scan=0), 4 RLS policies and 1 trigger.
findings.impact: Roughly 700 lines and a whole email+phone-OTP state machine that has never run once against production. It also carries an SMS OTP path — and the platform has a documented history of OTP delivery outages — that has never been proven end to end for this flow. This is not itself a bug; it is the single largest block of untested weight in this dimension.
findings.recommendation: Run one real invitation end to end (invite → email → OTP → complete) before the next org onboarding, or mark the flow explicitly unsupported and route staff onboarding through addOrgStaff. Drop the three never-scanned indexes (idx_organization_invitations_invited_by, organization_invitations_pkey usage aside, uq_organization_invitations_token) only after the flow is either proven or removed — the token index is load-bearing if it ever runs.

findings.title: No planner statistics exist for any table in the enterprise schema — all 14 have last_analyze AND last_autoanalyze NULL
findings.evidence: pg_stat_user_tables on live prod: all 13 organization_* tables plus funding_programs report last_vacuum, last_autovacuum, last_analyze and last_autoanalyze all NULL. pg_class.reltuples is -1 (never analyzed) for 10 of the 13: organization_billing_accounts, organization_disbursements, organization_group_access, organization_invitations, organization_journal_entries, organization_journal_lines, organization_ledger, organization_sms_credits, organization_subscriptions, organization_wallets, organizations. Dead-tuple ratios where writes did occur: organization_billing_accounts 100% (0 live / 2 dead), organization_sms_credits 100% (0/7), organization_disbursements 83% (1/5), organization_wallets 80% (1/4), funding_programs 75% (1/3), organizations 67% (1/2), organization_accounts 63% (3/5). This EXTENDS the already-banked never-autovacuumed finding (group_members, groups, welfare_requests, whatsapp_messages, credit_scores) to the entire enterprise schema.
findings.impact: Every plan touching these tables — listGroupSummaries' 4-LATERAL join, getOrganizationDetail's four-way fan-out, and the Configuration Service resolver's `organization_id IN (SELECT … FROM organization_group_access)` which runs 101 times in the pgss window — is built on Postgres' default selectivity guesses rather than real statistics. Harmless at 17 rows where any plan is optimal; it becomes a join-order hazard the moment a second organization with real linked-group volume arrives, and there is no autovacuum scheduled to correct it.
findings.recommendation: Run `ANALYZE` over the organization_* tables and funding_programs now (read-only from a planning standpoint, safe on prod), and investigate why autovacuum has never touched any of them — the pattern spanning both the enterprise and core schemas suggests a project-level autovacuum setting, not a per-table one.

findings.title: 44 of 76 indexes on organization tables have never been scanned, on tables holding 17 rows in total
findings.evidence: pg_stat_user_indexes filtered to organization_* + funding_programs: 76 indexes, 44 with idx_scan=0, ~700 kB. Worst offenders relative to content: organization_sms_credits has 6 indexes and 0 rows, 5 never scanned (idx_org_sms_credits_billing_account_id, idx_org_sms_credits_payment_id, organization_sms_credits_payment_id_key, organization_sms_credits_pkey, idx_org_sms_credits_added_by). organization_disbursements has 12 indexes for 1 row, 7 never scanned. organization_journal_entries has 6 for 1 row, 5 never scanned. organization_ledger has 7 for 2 rows, 5 never scanned. organization_group_access has 6 for 3 rows, 4 never scanned including idx_org_group_access_org_id — while idx_org_group_access_active (118 scans) and idx_org_group_access_group_id (49) carry all the traffic. Supabase's advisor independently reports 33 unused_index lints across these tables. Meanwhile organization_subscriptions has an unindexed FK (organization_subscriptions_assigned_by_fkey, advisor-confirmed) alongside an unused idx_org_subscriptions_org.
findings.impact: Write amplification and vacuum work on tables that barely write, plus ~700 kB. Small in absolute terms — this is index clutter, not a hot-path problem — but it is a third of the platform's 481-unused-index total concentrated in a schema serving one customer, and it makes the real access patterns harder to see.
findings.recommendation: Fold into the platform-wide unused-index sweep rather than treating separately. Two specific swaps worth making regardless: drop idx_org_group_access_org_id (0 scans; idx_org_group_access_active covers the same leading column) and add the missing covering index on organization_subscriptions(assigned_by), or drop the FK constraint if assignment provenance is only ever read from audit_logs.

findings.title: 9,200 lines of enterprise surface serve one organization, 17 rows, and fewer than 50 recorded query executions in 120 days
findings.evidence: Code: 5,422 lines across app/api/admin/organization (16 routes), app/api/admin/organizations (11 routes), app/api/v1/organization-invitations (5 routes), app/(enterprise) (11 pages), app/(admin)/admin/organizations (3 pages), components/enterprise; plus 3,791 lines across the 6 org services, organization-permissions.ts, organization.schema.ts, the accept-invite page, the enterprise login page and the ecosystem marketing page. Data: 1 organization (EZZAHCOMM, premium_plus, all caps NULL, monthly_fee 0.00), 2 staff, 3 linked groups, 1 funding program, 1 disbursement, 2 ledger rows, 1 journal entry, 3 chart-of-accounts rows, 1 wallet, 1 subscription, 0 invitations, 0 billing accounts, 0 sms credits — 17 rows across 13 tables. Traffic over the full pg_stat_statements window (stats_reset 2026-05-07, ~120 days): getWallet 8 calls, listGroupSummaries count 6, old dashboard rollup 5, listDisbursements 4, listLedger 3, getProfile 3, invitations list 3, listGroupSummaries LATERAL 2, programBudgetReport 2, donorSpendReport 2, trial balance 2, new group_stats dashboard 1, getEffectiveLimits 1, org members list 1, org branding SELECT 0, org-scoped audit_logs list 0 — roughly 42 executions total. Control run to falsify the zeroes: `%audit_logs al%` matches 57 calls elsewhere (the platform-wide admin list), and `%logo_url%` matches 24,033 calls, so the LIKE patterns do match live queries — the org-scoped variants are genuinely at zero.
findings.impact: Every one of these routes, pages, services, indexes and RLS policies must be kept compiling, migrated, permission-audited, and re-verified after every schema change — for a surface with effectively no users. It is the largest single concentration of carrying cost per unit of delivered value on the platform, and it is where the other findings in this report live.
findings.recommendation: This is a product decision, not an engineering one: either commit to selling the enterprise tier (in which case fix findings 1-4 first, since they are what a real customer would hit on day one) or freeze the surface — mark the unbuilt pages `soon: true`, stop scheduling the org SMS allowance job, and delete the dead route and mock data module. What should not continue is maintaining it at full weight while it serves one internal organization.
